description.en: Rice starch is derived from rice grains -Oryza sativa-, one of the world's most widely cultivated cereal crops, grown extensively across Asia, and increasingly in parts of the Americas and Europe. It is produced through wet milling, where rice is soaked, ground, and processed to separate starch from protein and other components, then dried into a fine white powder. Rice starch has a neutral, mildly sweet taste and a smooth, fine texture. It is valued in food manufacturing as a thickener, stabilizer, and texturizer in sauces, desserts, baked goods, and infant foods. Nutritionally, it is primarily composed of carbohydrates, offering an accessible energy source, with minimal fat, protein, or fiber content.

description.en: Millet is an ancient cereal grain domesticated in East Asia and Africa thousands of years ago, historically a staple in China, India, and parts of Africa long before rice and wheat became dominant. It has a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a light, fluffy texture when cooked, and a firmer, chewier bite when toasted first. It's naturally gluten-free and used in porridges, pilafs, flatbreads, and baked goods, offering a solid source of magnesium, phosphorus, fiber, and plant protein, along with antioxidants.

A sugar apple -also called sweetsop- is a tropical fruit from the Annona squamosa tree, native to the tropical Americas and West Indies. It has a bumpy, knobby green skin made up of overlapping segments that look almost like scales or a pinecone. When ripe, the segments separate easily. The white, creamy flesh inside is sweet and custard-like — hence "sugar" apple. The taste is often described as a blend of vanilla, pear, and banana, with a grainy, melt-in-your-mouth texture.

description.en: Native to Mexico and Guatemala, chia seeds come from the flowering plant Salvia hispanica. Black seeds are the traditional, more widely available variety; white seeds are a naturally occurring lighter variant, often prized for their appearance in pale-colored dishes. Both share a mild, nutty flavor and neutral taste, absorbing surrounding flavors easily. When soaked, they develop a gel-like texture, making them ideal for puddings, smoothies, baked goods, and as an egg substitute. Nutritionally identical, both are rich in fiber, plant-based omega-3s, protein, calcium, and antioxidants — a versatile, nutrient-dense addition to any diet.

Betel leaf -Piper betle- is a heart-shaped, glossy leaf native to Southeast Asia, now cultivated across South and Southeast Asia and parts of the Pacific. It has a pungent, peppery, slightly bitter flavor with an aromatic, faintly numbing quality from natural essential oils. Globally, it's best known as the wrapper for paan, but is also used to wrap savory bites -as in Thai miang kham-, chopped into chutneys, or used to wrap fish before steaming. Nutritionally, the leaf contains vitamins A and C, calcium, and trace minerals, along with aromatic compounds like eugenol and chavicol that contribute to its distinctive taste and traditional uses.

It has a mild, slightly sweet, neutral flavor with a texture that ranges from soft and fine -cake flour- to coarse and hearty -whole wheat-, largely defined by its protein and gluten content, which gives dough its characteristic elasticity and chew. description.en: Hydrolyzed vegetable protein -HVP- is a flavor enhancer made by chemically breaking down plant proteins—typically soy, corn, or wheat—using acid hydrolysis, a process developed in the early 20th century and widely adopted in industrial food manufacturing to create savory, meat-like flavors without meat. It has an intensely savory, umami-rich flavor with notes reminiscent of broth or bouillon, and comes as a fine powder or paste used in tiny quantities to boost taste. Commonly used in soups, sauces, snack seasonings, and processed foods as a cheaper alternative to natural flavor development, HVP contributes free glutamic acid -similar to MSG- along with trace amino acids, but is used in such small amounts that it offers negligible nutritional value beyond flavor enhancement.

SODIUM CHLORIDE commonly known as salt -though sea salt also contains other chemical salts-, is an ionic compound with the chemical formula NaCl, representing a 1:1 ratio of sodium and chloride ions. Salt is added to food, either by the food producer or by the consumer, as a flavor enhancer, preservative, binder, fermentation-control additive, texture-control agent and color developer.

description.en: Breadfruit is a starchy tropical fruit native to the South Pacific and Southeast Asia, long cultivated across Polynesian islands as a dietary staple, and historically significant for its role in the 18th-century Bounty voyage, which aimed to transplant it to the Caribbean as cheap food for enslaved laborers. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor reminiscent of fresh bread or potato when cooked, with a starchy, dense texture similar to a potato when roasted, boiled, or fried. Typically eaten cooked rather than raw, breadfruit is a good source of complex carbohydrates, fiber, potassium, and vitamin C, making it a nutrient-dense staple food in many tropical regions.

description.en: Soft red winter wheat is grown primarily in the eastern and central United States, planted in fall and harvested in early summer to take advantage of its cold-hardiness. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor with a subtle reddish-brown hue in the whole grain. Its low protein and gluten content make it well-suited for cakes, pastries, crackers, and flatbreads rather than yeasted bread. Nutritionally, it's mainly a carbohydrate source, with modest protein and fiber, especially in its refined form.

TOFU is a food prepared by coagulating soy milk and then pressing the resulting curds into solid white blocks of varying softness. Tofu has very little flavor or smell of its own. Consequently, tofu can be used in both savory or sweet dishes, acting as a bland background for presenting the flavors of the other ingredients used. In order to flavor the tofu it is often marinated in soy sauce, chillis, sesame oil, etc.

Bajra is one of India's oldest cultivated cereal grains, especially prominent in the arid and semi-arid regions of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana, and Maharashtra, where it thrives in low-rainfall, sandy soil conditions. The small, round grains range from pale yellow to grey, with an earthy, slightly nutty flavor. Bajra is traditionally ground into flour for rotis -bajra ki roti- and khichdi, or used whole in porridges, especially during winter months for its warming properties. Nutritionally, it's rich in fiber, iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, offers a good plant-protein source, and is naturally gluten-free—making it a staple in both everyday rural diets and gluten-free food formulations.

description.en: Tapioca pearls are made from cassava root starch, a plant native to South America but now cultivated widely across Brazil, Southeast Asia, and Africa. On their own, dry pearls are essentially flavorless and starchy, taking on a mild sweetness and chewy, translucent texture once cooked. Sea lettuce -Ulva lactuca and related Ulva species- is a bright green marine macroalga found in coastal waters worldwide, thriving in nutrient-rich shallows from the Atlantic and Pacific to the Mediterranean. It is harvested wild from rocky shores and increasingly cultivated in tanks, ponds, or ropes at sea, then washed, dried, or freeze-dried and milled. Its taste is mildly salty, fresh, and slightly grassy with oceanic umami. It is used in soups, salads, seasonings, snacks, and pastas across Asia, Europe, and the Americas. Nutritionally, it provides fiber, protein, iodine, iron, magnesium, and vitamins, while being naturally low in fat.

description.en: Trehalose is a naturally occurring disaccharide made of two glucose molecules, found in trace amounts in mushrooms, honey, and various plants and insects, and produced commercially today mainly through enzymatic conversion of starch, largely pioneered by Japanese researchers in the 1990s who made large-scale production affordable. It has a mild sweetness—roughly 45% as sweet as sucrose—with no notable aroma, and is valued in food processing for its exceptional stability, ability to protect texture and moisture in frozen or dried foods, and resistance to browning at high heat. Used in baked goods, frozen desserts, and dried fruits as a stabilizer and mild sweetener, trehalose provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, though it's digested more slowly than sucrose, giving it a gentler effect on blood sugar.

description.en: Oligofructose is a type of fructan—a short-chain fructose oligosaccharide—found naturally in plants like chicory root, onions, and bananas, and produced commercially mainly through partial enzymatic hydrolysis of chicory inulin, a process developed in Europe where chicory-based fibers are widely used. It has a mild sweetness, roughly 30-50% as sweet as sucrose, with a clean flavor and no notable aroma, and is used in food products as a low-calorie sweetener, fat replacer, and texture enhancer. Unlike simple sugars, oligofructose acts as a soluble prebiotic fiber that resists digestion in the small intestine and ferments in the colon, feeding beneficial gut bacteria while providing fewer calories than sucrose and supporting digestive health.

description.en: Glucose is a simple sugar -monosaccharide- that occurs naturally in fruits, honey, and plants, and is produced commercially by breaking down starch—typically from corn in the U.S. or wheat and potatoes in Europe—through enzymatic or acid hydrolysis. It has a moderately sweet flavor, less sweet than sucrose or fructose, with no notable aroma, and is available as a syrup or dried/powdered form used widely in candy-making, baking, and brewing for its resistance to crystallization and browning properties. As the primary fuel source for the human body, glucose provides purely caloric energy with no fiber, vitamins, or minerals, and it's the sugar that directly raises blood glucose levels, giving it the highest glycemic index among common sugars.

Chickpeas -Cicer arietinum-, also known as garbanzo beans, are one of the world's oldest cultivated legumes, originating in the Middle East over 7‚000 years ago and now grown widely across the Mediterranean, India, and the Americas. They have a mild, slightly nutty, earthy flavor with a firm yet creamy texture once cooked, making them extremely versatile in the kitchen. Chickpeas star in dishes like hummus, falafel, curries, soups, salads, and roasted snacks, and can be ground into flour for flatbreads and fritters. Nutritionally, they're a powerhouse: rich in plant-based protein, fiber, complex carbohydrates, iron, folate, and manganese, while being naturally low in fat. Their high fiber and protein content supports digestion, blood sugar stability, and satiety, making chickpeas a staple for vegetarian, vegan, and heart-healthy diets worldwide.

description.en: Ice is water in its solid state, forming when temperatures drop to or below 0°C -32°F-, found naturally in glaciers, polar regions, and frost, and produced commercially or at home through refrigeration for use in food and beverages. It has no flavor or aroma of its own, taking on a hard, crystalline texture that can range from clear and dense to cloudy and brittle depending on freezing speed and mineral content. Used primarily for chilling drinks and food, preserving perishables, and in ice sculptures or winter sports, ice contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, offering the same trace minerals as its source water but purely a physical, non-nutritive ingredient.

A synthetic salt manufactured industrially by reacting sodium hydroxide or sodium carbonate with nitrogen oxide gases, produced worldwide for food and industrial applications. It's typically supplied as a fine white to slightly yellowish crystalline powder. Sodium nitrite itself is essentially tasteless in the small quantities used, though it contributes to the characteristic tangy, savory flavor of cured meats through chemical reactions during processing. Widely used globally as a curing agent and preservative in bacon, ham, sausages, and other processed meats, where it inhibits bacterial growth -notably Clostridium botulinum- and stabilizes color. Nutritionally, it provides no caloric or nutrient value, serving solely a functional preservation role.

description.en: Red rice is a whole-grain rice variety that gets its reddish-brown hue from anthocyanin pigments in its bran layer, with well-known types grown in regions like Thailand, Bhutan, and the Camargue in France. It has a robust, earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a chewy, hearty texture, since the bran layer is left intact rather than polished away as with white rice. Naturally gluten-free, red rice is notably richer in fiber, antioxidants, and minerals like iron and magnesium than white rice, thanks to that retained bran layer.

description.en: A polysaccharide produced through fermentation of the bacterium Sphingomonas elodea, originally isolated from a pond in the United States and now manufactured globally, with major production in Asia and the Americas. It's made by fermenting sugar with the bacteria, then purifying and drying the resulting gum into a fine powder. Gellan gum is virtually tasteless and odorless, making it ideal as a texturizing agent. Widely used in dairy products, plant-based beverages, desserts, jams, and bakery items to provide gelling, thickening, and stabilizing properties. Nutritionally, it's a non-digestible fiber, contributing negligible calories and no significant vitamins or minerals to the diet.

description.en: L-CARNITINE is the left isomer of carnitine, a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants and some bacteria. The body synthesizes enough carnitine from lysine side chains to keep up with the needs of energy production in the body as carnitine acts as a transporter of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria to be oxidized and produce energy. Food sources rich in L-carnitine are animal products such as meat, poultry, fish, and milk. Redder meats tend to have higher levels of L-carnitine. Some individuals with genetic or medical disorders -like preterm infants- cannot make enough, so this makes carnitine a conditionally essential nutrient for them.

description.en: A sweet potato is a starchy root vegetable. It grows underground as a swollen root, It's skin can be orange, purple, white, or reddish; flesh is often orange, but also comes in white or purple. It has a naturally sweet flavor, especially when roasted or baked. It is rich in beta-carotene -converts to vitamin A- and a good source of fiber, vitamin C, potassium, and manganese, and has complex carbohydrates, so it digests more slowly than many other starches
ACETIC ACID, systematically named ethanoic acid, is a colourless liquid organic compound with the chemical formula CH3COOH -also written as CH3CO2H or C2H4O2-.

Yambean is a tropical legume -in the bean family, Fabaceae- grown primarily for its large, starchy, edible tuber/root. Native to Mexico and Central America, widely cultivated across Latin America and Southeast Asia. Mildly sweet, very crunchy, similar to a cross between an apple and a water chestnut — it stays crisp even when cooked.

"White-flowered gourd" -calabash- refers to Lagenaria siceraria — also known as bottle gourd, calabash gourd, opo squash, or long melon. It's the same plant whose hard-shelled fruits are dried and used as bottles, bowls, or musical instruments, but when eaten as food it's harvested young and tender, before the shell hardens. Very mild, slightly sweet, with a texture similar to zucchini or chayote — it takes on the flavor of whatever it's cooked with. Common in cuisines: South Asian -India, Pakistan, Bangladesh — called lauki, doodhi, or ghiya-, Chinese -hu lu-, Vietnamese, Italian -cucuzza-, and West African cooking. One caution worth knowing: bottle gourds can occasionally develop high levels of cucurbitacins -the compound that makes some gourds bitter-, which can cause food poisoning. The rule of thumb is — if it tastes bitter, don't eat it, even if just one bite.

description.en: Green gram, whole -Vigna radiata-, commonly known as mung bean or moong, originated in the Indian subcontinent and spread across Asia and beyond through centuries of trade and cultivation. Sold whole with its green skin intact, it has a mild, slightly sweet, earthy flavor and a firm texture that softens on cooking. It's used worldwide in soups, stews, curries, salads, and sprouts, and is especially popular in Asian cuisines from India to China and Southeast Asia. Nutritionally, it's rich in plant protein, dietary fiber, folate, potassium, and magnesium, making it a light, easily digestible legume valued globally for everyday and health-focused diets.

description.en: Brewing water is water specifically treated or selected for beer or coffee production, with mineral content—calcium, magnesium, sulfate, chloride, and bicarbonate—carefully adjusted to match regional styles, a practice tracing back to historic brewing centers like Burton-on-Trent -high sulfate, favoring hoppy pale ales- and Pilsen -very soft water, ideal for delicate lagers-. It has a neutral base flavor, but its mineral balance subtly shapes the final beverage's taste—sulfate accentuates hop bitterness and dryness, while chloride enhances malt sweetness and mouthfeel. Used as the primary ingredient in brewing -making up roughly 90-95% of beer-, water's mineral profile is often adjusted through filtration, dilution, or targeted mineral additions to achieve consistency and match desired beer or coffee styles. As with plain water, brewing water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, only trace minerals that influence flavor rather than nutrition.

description.en: Buckwheat, despite its name, isn't a wheat relative at all—it's a fruit seed related to rhubarb, originating in Central Asia and cultivated in China for thousands of years before spreading through Europe and Russia. Its groats have an earthy, nutty flavor with a slight bitterness that deepens when toasted -as in kasha-, and they're used whole, ground into flour, or sprouted in dishes ranging from soba noodles to porridge and pancakes. Naturally gluten-free, buckwheat is a good source of plant protein, fiber, magnesium, and manganese, plus rutin, an antioxidant linked to cardiovascular benefits.

Oats are a cereal grain that originated in Western Asia or Europe, historically used as animal fodder before rising to prominence as a hearty breakfast staple, especially in Scotland and Northern Europe. They have a mild, creamy, subtly sweet flavor with a soft, chewy texture that varies by processing—from firm steel-cut to quick-cooking rolled or instant forms. Oats are naturally gluten-free -though often cross-contaminated during processing- and are notable for their beta-glucan fiber, which supports heart health, along with solid amounts of protein, manganese, and iron.

description.en: Epazote -Dysphania ambrosioides, formerly Chenopodium ambrosioides- is a pungent, aromatic herb widely used in Mexican and Central American cooking. The flavor is hard to pin down — people describe it as a mix of citrus, mint, anise, tar, and even petroleum-like notes. It's strong, so it's used in moderation, usually just a sprig or a few leaves per dish, added toward the end of cooking to preserve its aroma. Epazote contains compounds -like ascaridole- that can be toxic in concentrated amounts, such as in essential oil form. Using fresh or dried leaves in normal cooking quantities is considered safe and is how it's traditionally consumed — but it shouldn't be consumed as a concentrated extract or in medicinal "high dose" preparations.

description.en: Bulgur is a parboiled wheat product made by steaming or boiling whole wheat kernels, drying them, then cracking them into coarse or fine granules. Originating in the Middle East/Mediterranean region thousands of years ago -a staple in Levantine and Turkish cuisine-, it retains the bran and germ since it's made from whole wheat. It has a mild, nutty, slightly toasty taste and a light, fluffy texture once rehydrated. Used in tabbouleh, pilafs, soups, and as a quick-cooking rice substitute. Nutritionally, it's high in fiber and protein, with more iron, magnesium, and B-vitamins retained than refined flour, and a moderate glycemic index.

"Cloud ear" -also called wood ear, black fungus, or mù'ěr 木耳 in Chinese- refers to mushrooms in the genus Auricularia — most commonly Auricularia auricula-judae or Auricularia cornea. They're a type of jelly fungus that grows on decaying or living wood, especially elder, beech, and other broadleaf trees. Cloud ears are prized more for their texture than flavor — they're crunchy, slightly gelatinous, and almost cartilaginous when cooked, but have very little taste of their own. That makes them great at soaking up other flavors in a dish.

description.en: MALTITOL is a sugar alcohol -a polyol- used as a sugar substitute. It has 75–90% of the sweetness of sucrose -table sugar- and nearly identical properties, except for browning. Maltitol's high sweetness allows it to be used without being mixed with other sweeteners. It is used in candy manufacture, particularly sugar-free hard candy, chewing gum, chocolates, baked goods, and ice cream.

Native to the prairies and open woodlands of central and eastern North America, purple coneflower has long been used by Indigenous peoples before spreading globally as a cultivated herb. Today it's grown commercially across North America, Europe, and parts of Asia, with roots, leaves, and flowers harvested, dried, and processed into powders, extracts, teas, or tinctures. Its flavor is earthy, slightly bitter, and mildly tingling on the tongue. It's used in herbal teas, tinctures, capsules, and functional foods/beverages worldwide. Nutritionally, it contains polysaccharides, flavonoids, alkylamides, and trace vitamins and minerals, though it's consumed in small quantities as a flavoring or functional additive rather than a significant caloric or macronutrient source.

Milkfish -Chanos chanos- is a mild-flavored, silvery fish that's a staple food in parts of Southeast Asia, especially the Philippines, Indonesia, and Taiwan. Texture and flavor: The flesh is soft, slightly fatty, and has a mild taste that takes on marinades and seasonings well. It's notoriously bony, with many small, fine bones running through the flesh. This has led to specialty products like "boneless milkfish," where the bones are removed before selling.

The LEEK is a vegetable, a cultivar of Allium ampeloprasum, the broadleaf wild leek. Leeks have a mild, onion-like taste. In its raw state, the vegetable is crunchy and firm. The edible portions of the leek are the white base of the leaves -above the roots and stem base-, the light green parts, and to a lesser extent the dark green parts of the leaves. Leeks are typically chopped into slices 5–10 mm thick. The slices have a tendency to fall apart, due to the layered structure of the leek. The different ways of preparing the vegetable are: boiling, frying or raw.

Cowpeas -Vigna unguiculata-, also known as black-eyed peas or southern peas, originated in West Africa thousands of years ago before spreading to the Mediterranean, Asia, and the Americas via trade and slavery routes. They have an earthy, mildly nutty flavor with a creamy texture once cooked. Versatile in the kitchen, they're used in stews, salads, fritters -like akara-, rice dishes -such as Hoppin' John-, and purees. Nutritionally, cowpeas are a powerhouse: high in plant-based protein and fiber, rich in folate, iron, magnesium, and potassium, and naturally low in fat—making them a staple for heart-healthy, budget-friendly diets worldwide.

Tilefish is a type of saltwater fish found mainly in the western Atlantic Ocean, from the northeastern U.S. down through the Gulf of Mexico. There are a few species, but the most commonly eaten ones are golden tilefish -also called "white tilefish" in markets- and blueline tilefish. Flavor and texture: Mild, sweet flavor with firm, moist flesh — often compared to a cross between lobster and crab in taste, which is why it's sometimes nicknamed "poor man's lobster." The texture holds up well to various cooking methods. Cooking methods: It works well baked, roasted, pan-seared, grilled, or poached. The skin can be crisped up nicely in a pan. It's popular in Japanese cuisine too, where it's called amadai and often prepared with the scales left on and fried until crispy.

MALTOSE, also known as maltobiose or malt sugar, is a disaccharide formed from two units of glucose joined. Maltose is a component of malt, a substance which is obtained in the process of allowing grain to soften in water and germinate. It is also present in highly variable quantities in partially hydrolysed starch products like maltodextrin, corn syrup and acid-thinned starch. In humans, maltose is broken down by various maltase enzymes, providing two glucose molecules which can be further processed: either broken down to provide energy, or stored as glycogen. The lack of the sucrase-isomaltase enzyme in humans causes sucrose intolerance.

description.en: Soy comes from the soybean, a legume domesticated in China around 3‚000-5‚000 years ago and long a dietary staple across East Asia, later spreading globally as both a food crop and major agricultural commodity. It has a mild, earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a texture that varies enormously by form—from the firm bite of tofu and edamame to the smooth creaminess of soy milk and the meaty chew of tempeh. Extremely versatile, soy is used in countless forms including tofu, milk, sauce, and protein isolates, and stands out nutritionally as a complete plant protein containing all nine essential amino acids, along with fiber, iron, and isoflavones linked to potential health benefits.

description.en: Carbonated water is water infused with dissolved carbon dioxide gas under pressure, either occurring naturally in mineral springs—historically prized in spa towns like Perrier in France—or produced artificially through mechanical carbonation, a process commercialized in the late 18th century. It has a neutral base flavor with a distinctive sharp, slightly acidic bite and effervescent tingle from the carbonic acid formed as CO2 dissolves, and a lively, fizzy texture that fades once opened. Used as a refreshing standalone drink, a mixer in cocktails, and a base for flavored sodas, carbonated water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, and offers the same trace minerals as its source water, with no meaningful nutritional difference from still water beyond the carbonation itself.

The term lecithin refers to a group of compounds found in every living organism, as they are part of the cell wall of all cells. Lecithin is commercially isolated -mainly- from soybeans or egg yolk.

Cranberries come in two main varieties: the American cranberry -Vaccinium macrocarpon-, native to North America and long used by Indigenous peoples before becoming a major commercial crop in states like Massachusetts and Wisconsin, and the smaller European cranberry -Vaccinium oxycoccos-, native to boggy regions across Northern Europe and Asia and traditionally foraged rather than farmed. Both have a sharply tart, astringent flavor with a firm, crisp bite when fresh, though the European variety tends to be smaller and even more tart than its larger American cousin. Eaten fresh, dried, juiced, or made into sauces, cranberries are notably rich in antioxidants, vitamin C, and compounds linked to urinary tract health, making them valued more for their functional benefits than their raw palatability.

description.en: Durian is a large, spiky tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia, particularly Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand, where it's been cultivated for centuries and earned the nickname "king of fruits" despite—or because of—its notoriously divisive smell. It has a custardy, rich, creamy texture with a complex flavor often described as a blend of sweet caramel, almond, and savory onion notes, paired with a famously pungent, sulfurous odor strong enough to be banned on public transport in parts of Southeast Asia. Eaten fresh or used in desserts, candies, and ice cream, durian is notably rich in healthy fats, fiber, vitamin C, and potassium, making it more calorie-dense and nutritious than most other fruits.

description.en: Ascorbic acid is a naturally occurring organic compound found in citrus fruits, berries, and vegetables such as peppers and broccoli. Commercially, it is produced industrially through fermentation of glucose -often derived from corn-, followed by chemical conversion steps, yielding a highly pure, food-grade powder. It has a mildly tart, sour taste, similar to citrus. Ascorbic acid is widely used as a food additive -E300- for its antioxidant properties, preventing browning and preserving freshness in juices, canned goods, and processed foods. Nutritionally, it is an essential water-soluble vitamin, contributing to collagen synthesis, immune function, and iron absorption across diverse global diets.

description.en: Carnitine is a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants and some bacteria. The body synthesizes enough carnitine from lysine side chains to keep up with the needs of energy production in the body as carnitine acts as a transporter of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria to be oxidized and produce energy. Food sources rich in L-carnitine are animal products such as meat, poultry, fish, and milk. Redder meats tend to have higher levels of L-carnitine. Some individuals with genetic or medical disorders -like preterm infants- cannot make enough, so this makes carnitine a conditionally essential nutrient for them.

Samai, or little millet -Panicum sumatrense, syn. Panicum miliare-, is one of India's oldest cultivated minor millets, traditionally grown in the rain-fed hills and plateaus of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Odisha for over 5‚000 years. Its small, round grains carry a mild, subtly nutty flavor and light, fluffy texture when cooked. Valued for its resilience in poor soil and low rainfall, it's traditionally used as a rice substitute—steamed, boiled into porridge -kanji-, or ground into idli and dosa batters—and is popular during religious fasting periods. Nutritionally, samai is rich in dietary fiber, iron, and B vitamins, has a low glycemic index, and is naturally gluten-free, making it valued in diabetic-friendly and gluten-free diets.

description.en: Originating in the Fertile Crescent over 8‚000 years ago, lentils spread across the Mediterranean, Middle East, South Asia, and beyond, becoming a dietary cornerstone worldwide. Known as "dal" in South Asia, they come in many varieties—red, green, brown, black, yellow—each with subtly different flavor, from mild and sweet to earthy. Quick-cooking and hulling-friendly, lentils are simmered into soups, stews, curries, and purées across cuisines, from Indian dal tadka to French lentille du Puy salads and Middle Eastern mujadara. Nutritionally, they're a powerhouse of plant protein, fiber, iron, and folate, making them a global staple for sustainable, affordable nutrition.

description.en: Baker's yeast is the common name for active Saccharomyces cerevisiae used specifically for baking, cultivated commercially since the late 19th century when compressed yeast production made it widely accessible, replacing older methods like sourdough starters and brewer's yeast. It has a mild, slightly savory flavor with little aroma on its own, though it develops the characteristic yeasty, bready aroma during fermentation, and is sold as fresh -compressed-, active dry, or instant granules. Used to leaven bread, rolls, and pastries, baker's yeast works by converting sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol, and while used in small quantities, it contributes trace amounts of B vitamins and protein alongside its primary leavening function.

description.en: Maida is a highly refined wheat flour, milled from Triticum aestivum after the bran and germ are removed, leaving mostly starchy endosperm — a process that became widespread in India with industrial roller-milling. It has a mild, slightly sweet, neutral taste, making it a versatile base that readily takes on other flavors. Maida is used for naan, bhatura, puri, pastries, cakes, biscuits, and samosa wrappers, prized for its soft, elastic texture. Nutritionally, it's calorie-dense -~348 kcal/100g- but low in fiber and micronutrients -iron, zinc, B-vitamins-, with a high glycemic index compared to whole wheat flour.

description.en: Fructose is a simple sugar -monosaccharide- that occurs naturally in fruits, honey, and some vegetables, and is produced commercially either by processing corn starch into high-fructose corn syrup -mainly in the U.S.- or by refining it from sucrose. It has the sweetest taste of all natural sugars—notably sweeter than sucrose or glucose—with no notable aroma, and is used in beverages, baked goods, and processed foods both for its intense sweetness and its ability to enhance flavor and browning. Fructose provides purely empty calories with no fiber, vitamins, or minerals, and is metabolized differently than glucose—processed primarily by the liver—which has made it a focus of concern around excessive consumption and links to metabolic issues.

description.en: Melado is an unrefined liquid sugar syrup made from concentrated sugarcane juice, a traditional product especially common in Brazil and other Latin American countries where it's produced as a byproduct or lighter-processed cousin of molasses, retaining more of the cane's natural sweetness. It has a rich, deep caramel flavor with molasses-like notes but milder and less bitter than true molasses, and a thick, syrupy texture. description.en: Native to Central and South America, amaranth was a staple grain of the Aztec and Inca civilizations, prized for its resilience and nutritional density. Black amaranth seeds have a mild, earthy, slightly peppery flavor with a subtle nuttiness that intensifies when toasted or popped. Versatile in the kitchen, they can be cooked like porridge, popped for snacking or garnishing, ground into flour for gluten-free baking, or sprouted for salads and bowls. Nutritionally, amaranth is a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, including lysine—rare among grains. It's also rich in fiber, iron, magnesium, and manganese, and naturally gluten-free, making it a nutrient-dense choice for ancient-grain and health-focused products.

comment.en: USDA NDB 20001 is a generic entry covering amaranth grain broadly -species like Amaranthus cruentus, hypochondriacus, or caudatus-, not specifically black-seeded varieties. "Black amaranth" usually refers to darker-seeded cultivars -sometimes ornamental/wild types like Amaranthus hybridus-, which can differ slightly in flavor -often described as more bitter/earthy than the common cream-colored grain amaranth- and are less commonly the ones used in commercial food products.

description.en: Psyllium is the seed husk of Plantago ovata, a plant part grown mainly in India -the world's dominant producer-, with smaller output in Pakistan, Iran, and parts of Europe. Seeds are harvested and cleaned, then the husk is mechanically separated by milling and sifting, and sometimes ground into powder, without extraction or chemical treatment. It is nearly tasteless, with a slightly mucilaginous texture. It is used as a binder and gelling agent in gluten-free baking, as a thickener, and in fiber supplements and cereals. Nutritionally, it is about 70 to 85% soluble fiber, providing roughly 0 to 2 kcal/g, with negligible fat and protein.

description.es: Cynara scolymus, la alcachofera, alcachofa, alcacil o alcaucil,1​ entre otros numerosos nombres vernáculos, es una planta herbácea del género Cynara en la familia Asteraceae; es cultivada desde la antigüedad como alimento en climas templados.
description.en: The globe ARTICHOKE -Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus-, also known as French artichoke and green artichoke in the USA, is a variety of a species of thistle cultivated as a food. Leaves are often removed one at a time, and the fleshy base eaten, with hollandaise, vinegar, butter, mayonnaise, aioli, lemon juice, or other sauces. The fibrous upper part of each leaf is usually discarded. The heart is eaten when the inedible choke has been peeled away from the base and discarded. The thin leaves covering the choke are also edible.
description.de: Die Artischocke -Cynara cardunculus subsp. scolymus -L.- Hegi, Syn.: Cynara scolymus L.- ist eine distelartige, kräftige Kulturpflanze aus der Familie der Korbblütler. description.en: Basella alba, commonly called Malabar spinach or vine spinach, is a fast-growing climbing vine native to tropical Asia and Africa, now cultivated widely across South and Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean. Its thick, glossy leaves have a mild, slightly peppery taste and a mucilaginous texture similar to okra when cooked. Popular in stir-fries, soups, curries, and stews, it holds up well in hot, humid climates where true spinach struggles. Nutritionally, the leaves are rich in vitamins A and C, iron, calcium, and antioxidants, with a naturally high water and fiber content, making them a staple leafy green in many traditional cuisines worldwide.

description.en: CHORIZO or chouriço is a type of pork sausage. In Europe, chorizo is a fermented, cured, smoked sausage, which may be sliced and eaten without cooking, or added as an ingredient to add flavor to other dishes. Elsewhere, some sausages sold as chorizo may not be fermented and cured, and require cooking before eating. Spanish chorizo and Portuguese chouriço get their distinctive smokiness and deep red color from dried, smoked, red peppers.

description.en: Water is a naturally occurring compound of hydrogen and oxygen, found throughout the environment in oceans, rivers, lakes, and groundwater, and sourced for consumption from municipal supplies, wells, springs, and glaciers depending on region. It has a neutral, essentially flavorless and odorless profile, though mineral content can lend subtle differences—spring water often tastes slightly mineral-rich, while distilled water tastes notably flat. As the foundation of virtually all food and beverage preparation, water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, though mineral or spring varieties may carry trace amounts of minerals like calcium, magnesium, and potassium, and it remains essential for nearly every bodily function.

Its flavor is peppery and slightly sweet when raw, mellowing into a tangy, earthy sweetness when cooked, often enhanced with vinegar or apples in European cuisines. Globally, it's eaten raw in salads and slaws, pickled, fermented, braised, or stewed alongside meats in German, Scandinavian, and Eastern European dishes. Nutritionally, it's a good source of vitamin C, vitamin K, fiber, and various antioxidant compounds, contributing to its widespread culinary and cultural presence.

description.en: Dietary fiber is the indigestible carbohydrate portion of plant foods, produced worldwide from cereals -oats, wheat, rice-, legumes -peas, soy-, fruits -citrus, apple-, roots -chicory, sugar beet- and sugarcane residues. Production involves collecting by-products or plant parts, washing, extracting or milling, drying, and sometimes bleaching or purifying to a fine powder. Its taste is neutral to slightly sweet or grainy. Industries use it to add bulk, retain moisture, thicken, replace fat or sugar, and improve texture in bakery, meat, dairy, and beverage products. Nutritionally, it provides little to no digestible energy -0 to 2 kcal/g-, and can be soluble or insoluble.

description.en: Brown sugar is sugar—typically from sugarcane—that retains or has molasses added back in during processing, a practice with roots in unrefined "raw" sugars historically produced across the Caribbean, South Asia, and other cane-growing regions before fully refined white sugar became standard. It has a rich, warm, caramel-like flavor with subtle toffee and mineral notes from the molasses, and a moist, clumping texture ranging from light to dark depending on molasses content. Commonly used in baking, glazes, and sauces for its depth and moisture, brown sugar offers only trace minerals like calcium and iron from the molasses, making it nutritionally almost identical to white sugar—still primarily empty calories.

description.en: Native to South Asia, horse gram is an ancient, drought-resistant legume long cultivated across India, Nepal, and parts of Africa and Southeast Asia, where it's also used as livestock fodder. Small, flattish, and reddish-brown, it has a robust, earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a firm bite. Traditionally simmered into soups, stews, and sprouted dishes, or ground into flour, it's especially prized in South Indian cuisine -like kulith usal-. Nutritionally, it stands out among pulses for its exceptional protein, iron, and calcium content, along with dietary fiber, making it a valued, if underappreciated, global superfood.

description.en: Sugar -sucrose- comes from sugarcane, first domesticated in New Guinea thousands of years ago and later spread through Asia and the Middle East to become the dominant global source, and from sugar beet, which took hold in Europe after Napoleon's early 1800s Continental Blockade cut off cane sugar imports and spurred domestic beet production, making it the region's primary source today. It has a pure, intensely sweet flavor with no notable aroma, available in forms ranging from fine granulated and powdered sugar to coarser raw and brown sugars with mild molasses notes. Used universally in baking, cooking, preserving, and sweetening beverages, sugar provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, making it a source of energy without nutritional value.

comment.en: Generic sugar is vegan:maybe because some cane sugar is refined using bone char -charred cattle bones- as a decolorizing filter. This is primarily a North American practice. Beet sugar, organic sugar, and unrefined sugars never use bone char. Vegetarian status remains yes as bone char is a processing aid and the final product contains no animal-derived material.

description.en: GUM BASE is the non-nutritive, non-digestible, water-insoluble masticatory delivery system used to carry sweeteners, flavors, and any other substances in chewing gum and bubble gum. SPARKLING WINE is a wine with significant levels of carbon dioxide in it, making it fizzy. Sparkling wine is usually either white or rosé, but there are examples of red sparkling wines.

Cottonseed is the seed of the cotton plant -genus Gossypium-, harvested as a byproduct of cotton fiber production. After cotton bolls are picked, the fluffy fiber -lint- is separated from the seeds during a process called ginning. Each cotton boll contains several seeds embedded in the fiber. Raw cottonseed contains a natural compound called gossypol, which is toxic to humans in significant quantities. Some specialty "glandless" cotton varieties have been bred to have naturally low gossypol levels, and these are sometimes explored as a protein source -the seed kernel is fairly protein-rich-, but this isn't mainstream or widely available commercially.

description.en: An organic acid naturally occurring in fermented foods, first identified in sour milk, now produced globally through microbial fermentation. It's manufactured by fermenting carbohydrate sources like corn, sugarcane, or beets with lactic acid bacteria, followed by purification. Lactic acid has a sharp, tangy, sour taste and is used worldwide as an acidulant, preservative, and pH regulator in dairy products, baked goods, beverages, pickled vegetables, and processed meats. It also aids fermentation in foods like yogurt and sauerkraut. Nutritionally, it provides a negligible caloric contribution and no significant vitamins or minerals, functioning primarily as a flavoring and preservation agent rather than a nutrient source.

Sweet corn is a cultivar of maize -Zea mays var. saccharata- bred to accumulate higher natural sugar content, harvested young and tender before the kernels mature and starch fully develops. Compared to local field maize, it has a distinctly sweeter, juicier taste with a crisp, tender bite. Popular worldwide, sweet corn is boiled or steamed on the cob, grilled, or used kernel-off-cob in salads, soups, stir-fries, and Indian street snacks like corn chaat. Nutritionally, it offers dietary fiber, carbohydrates, and moderate protein, along with vitamin C, B vitamins -especially folate-, magnesium, and antioxidants such as lutein and zeaxanthin, which support eye health. Its natural sweetness also makes it a favorite in both savory and lightly sweetened preparations.

description.en: MONOSODIUM GLUTAMATE -MSG, also known as sodium glutamate- is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, one of the most abundant naturally occurring non-essential amino acids.

wikipedia_abstract.fr: Le glutamate monosodique, également connu sous le nom de glutamate de sodium, monosodium glutamate, GMS ou MSG, est le sel sodique de l'acide glutamique, l'un des acides aminés non essentiels les plus abondants dans la nature. La FDA -organisme américain de surveillance des aliments et des médicaments- a classé le GMS comme « GRAS », généralement reconnu inoffensif, et l'Union européenne l'a classé comme additif alimentaire mais l'ajout de glutamates n'y est pas autorisé dans le lait, les huiles et les émulsions de graisse, les pâtes, le cacao et les produits chocolatés, les jus de fruits. Le GMS possède le numéro E621. Le glutamate du GMS confère le même goût umami que le glutamate issu d'autres aliments. Les fabricants de produits alimentaires commercialisent et utilisent le GMS comme exhausteur de goût car il équilibre, mélange et arrondit la perception globale des autres goûts,. Les dénominations commerciales du glutamate monosodique comprennent AJI-NO-MOTO®, Vetsin et Ac'cent.
wikipedia_abstract.en: Monosodium glutamate -MSG, also known as sodium glutamate- is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, one of the most abundant naturally occurring non-essential amino acids. Glutamic acid is found naturally in tomatoes, grapes, cheese, mushrooms and other foods.MSG is used in the food industry as a flavor enhancer with an umami taste that intensifies the meaty, savory flavor of food, as naturally occurring glutamate does in foods such as stews and meat soups. It was first prepared in 1908 by Japanese biochemist Kikunae Ikeda, who was trying to isolate and duplicate the savory taste of kombu, an edible seaweed used as a base for many Japanese soups. MSG as a flavor enhancer balances, blends, and rounds the perception of other tastes.The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has given MSG its generally recognized as safe -GRAS- designation. A popular belief is that large doses of MSG can cause headaches and other feelings of discomfort, known as "Chinese restaurant syndrome," but double-blind tests fail to find evidence of such a reaction. The European Union classifies it as a food additive permitted in certain foods and subject to quantitative limits. MSG has the HS code 29224220 and the E number E621.

description.en: Varagu, known in English as kodo millet, is another of India's ancient minor millets, cultivated for over 3‚000 years primarily in the drier, hilly regions of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, and Chhattisgarh. It's one of the hardiest millets, thriving in poor soils with minimal water, and is often grown as a famine-reserve or marginal-land crop. The small, round, reddish-brown grains have an earthy, mildly nutty flavor similar to other millets. Traditionally cooked like rice, ground into flour for flatbreads, or used in porridges and idli/dosa batters, it's also popular in fasting foods and diabetic-friendly diets. Nutritionally, kodo millet is notably high in dietary fiber and polyphenol antioxidants, a good source of iron and B vitamins, naturally gluten-free, and has one of the lowest glycemic indices among cereals.

description.en: Dock -genus Rumex, especially curly dock — Rumex crispus — and broad-leaved dock — Rumex obtusifolius- is a wild edible plant. Young leaves have a tart, lemony, slightly sour flavor thanks to oxalic acid — similar to sorrel but a bit milder. As leaves mature they get tougher and more bitter/astringent. Young leaves: eaten raw in salads, or added to soups, stews, and sautés like spinach.; Older leaves: usually cooked -boiled or braised- to mellow the sourness and soften the texture.

BOSTON BUTT, or pork butt, is the American name for a cut of pork that comes from the upper part of the shoulder from the front leg and may contain the blade bone.  Boston butt is the most common cut used for pulled pork, a staple of barbecue in the southern United States.

Yeast extract is a savory paste or powder made by breaking down yeast cells—typically through autolysis -self-digestion using the yeast's own enzymes- or hydrolysis—a byproduct process refined in the late 19th century that led to iconic products like Marmite in the UK and Vegemite in Australia. It has an intensely savory, salty, umami-rich flavor with deep, almost meaty notes, and comes as a thick, sticky spread or dried into a fine powder used as a seasoning. Used as a flavor enhancer in soups, sauces, stocks, and spreads, yeast extract is naturally rich in glutamic acid -contributing its umami punch-, B vitamins, and protein, making it both a flavor booster and a modest nutritional contributor.

description.en: Rolled oats are whole oat groats that have been steamed and pressed flat with large rollers, a processing method developed in the late 1800s to shorten cooking time while keeping the grain mostly intact. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a soft, chewy texture that holds its shape better than instant oats, making them the classic choice for traditional oatmeal, granola, and baking. Like other oats, they're naturally gluten-free -if uncontaminated- and rich in beta-glucan fiber for heart health, plus protein, manganese, and iron, though their nutrition is nearly identical to whole oats since minimal processing preserves the bran and germ.

It is primarily used as an additive in infant formula, nutritional supplements, and functional foods across global markets, valued for standardized quality and non-animal, non-fish origin. S. cerevisiae is used in baking; the carbon dioxide generated by the fermentation is used as a leavening agent in bread and other baked goods. Historically, this use was closely linked to the brewing industry's use of yeast, as bakers took or bought the barm or yeast-filled foam from brewing ale from the brewers -producing the barm cake-; today, brewing and baking yeast strains are somewhat different.

description.en: Fiddlehead ferns are the tightly coiled, immature fronds of certain fern species, harvested in early spring before they unfurl. They're named for their resemblance to the curled end -scroll- of a fiddle or violin. Most common edible variety: Ostrich fern -Matteuccia struthiopteris- is the safest and most widely eaten species. Not all fern fiddleheads are edible — some are toxic, so identification matters. Often described as a cross between asparagus, green beans, and a slightly nutty, grassy taste. Fiddleheads must be cooked thoroughly -boiled or steamed for several minutes, then sautéed if desired- before eating. Raw or undercooked fiddleheads have caused foodborne illness outbreaks — they can carry bacteria or contain compounds that cause nausea, cramps, and diarrhea if not properly prepared.

Chinese broccoli -also called gai lan or kai lan, 芥蓝- is actually a distinct vegetable from regular broccoli, though they're related. Both belong to the Brassica oleracea species and the broader cabbage family. Gai lan has long, thick green stalks with flat, broad leaves and small, scattered flower buds. Quinoa is an ancient pseudocereal native to the Andean region of South America, cultivated by the Incas for thousands of years and revered as a sacred "mother grain." It has a light, slightly nutty and earthy flavor with a delicate crunch, and its grains form a small, curled tail when cooked that gives it a distinctive texture. Naturally gluten-free, quinoa is notable for being a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, and it's also a good source of fiber, iron, magnesium, and manganese.

Caseinate is a soluble form of casein—typically sodium or calcium caseinate—created by treating milk casein with an alkali to make it water-soluble, a processing method developed in the early-to-mid 20th century to allow casein's functional properties to be used more easily in manufactured foods. It has a neutral, mildly milky flavor with no strong aroma, and unlike regular casein, it dissolves smoothly in liquids and forms stable emulsions rather than clumping into curds. Widely used as an emulsifier and protein fortifier in coffee creamers, processed cheeses, and protein supplements, caseinate remains a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, along with calcium and phosphorus from its dairy origin.

description.en: Green cabbage -Brassica oleracea var. capitata- originated in the Mediterranean and Western Europe, cultivated from wild mustard plants over 2‚000 years ago before spreading worldwide through trade and colonization. Today it's a staple across Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas. Its tightly packed, pale-green leaves offer a crisp texture and mild, slightly peppery flavor that turns sweeter when cooked, with a subtle sulfurous note. Used raw in slaws and salads, fermented into sauerkraut and kimchi, or cooked in soups, stir-fries, stews, and stuffed dishes, it adapts to countless culinary traditions. Nutritionally, green cabbage provides vitamin C, vitamin K, fiber, and small amounts of various minerals, while being low in calories.

description.en: Amaranth leaves come from the amaranth plant, native to Central and South America but now cultivated widely across Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean, where they form a staple leafy vegetable. Varieties range from vivid red-purple to deep green, with spined and spineless forms differing mainly in stem texture. The leaves have a mild, slightly earthy, spinach-like flavor with a subtle sweetness. They're commonly boiled, steamed, sautéed, or added to soups, stews, and stir-fries, softening quickly when cooked. Nutritionally, amaranth leaves are notably rich in vitamins A, C, and K, folate, calcium, iron, and dietary fiber, alongside plant-based protein.

Widely enjoyed as street food, it's traditionally roasted over open coals and rubbed with lime, chili, and salt -bhutta-, boiled as a snack, or grated into curries, soups, and flatbreads. Nutritionally, tender maize provides dietary fiber, complex carbohydrates, and moderate protein, along with B vitamins, magnesium, and antioxidants like lutein and zeaxanthin, making it a wholesome seasonal staple across India.

description.en: Nutritional yeast is a deactivated form of Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast, typically grown on molasses and then heat-killed before being dried into flakes or powder, popularized in the mid-20th century as a health food, particularly within vegan and vegetarian communities. It has a distinctly savory, cheesy, nutty flavor with umami depth, making it a popular seasoning sprinkled over popcorn, pasta, and salads or blended into vegan cheese sauces. description.en: Triticale is a hybrid grain bred by crossing wheat and rye, first developed in the late 19th century and refined for commercial use in Europe through the 20th century. Its flour has an earthy, nutty flavor that combines wheat's mildness with rye's slight tanginess. It's used to make breads, pastas, and crackers, often blended with other flours for improved texture and rise. Nutritionally, whole-grain triticale flour is high in fiber, protein, and minerals like magnesium and iron, though it still contains gluten.

Breadnut -also called kamansi in the Philippines, or "chataigne" in the Caribbean- produces large, spiky green fruits similar in appearance to breadfruit, but unlike the common seedless breadfruit variety, breadnut fruits are packed with edible seeds — usually 100+ per fruit. The seeds themselves are roughly the size of chestnuts or large beans. Typically boiled, roasted, or steamed before eating. After cooking, the texture is starchy and nutty, often compared to chestnuts or roasted potatoes.

Corn flour comes from maize, a grain domesticated in southern Mexico around 9‚000 years ago and later becoming a dietary cornerstone across the Americas, from Mexican tortillas to Southern U.S. cornbread. It has a mild, slightly sweet, distinctly corn flavor with a fine, slightly gritty texture that lends baked goods a tender crumb and golden color. Naturally gluten-free, corn flour offers decent fiber and is a good source of B vitamins and antioxidants like lutein and zeaxanthin, though its protein is incomplete and lower in quality compared to grains like quinoa.

description.en: Invert sugar is a liquid sugar syrup produced by splitting sucrose into its component parts—glucose and fructose—through hydrolysis using heat, acid, or enzymes, a process discovered in the 19th century and now widely used in food manufacturing rather than home kitchens. It has a flavor sweeter than regular sugar -since fructose tastes sweeter than sucrose- with a smooth, syrupy texture, and it's prized in baking and confectionery for resisting crystallization, retaining moisture, and extending shelf life in products like candies, jams, and soft baked goods. Like other sugars, invert sugar provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, offering energy without nutritional value.

Yeast is a single-celled fungus, most commonly Saccharomyces cerevisiae, used for thousands of years since ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian times to leaven bread and ferment beverages like beer and wine, long before its microbial nature was understood. It has a mild, slightly savory, umami flavor with a subtly yeasty, bread-like aroma, and comes in fresh, active dry, or instant forms that vary in texture from soft and crumbly to fine granules. Used in baking, brewing, and winemaking, yeast works by converting sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol through fermentation, and nutritional yeast -a deactivated form- is notably rich in B vitamins, protein, and often fortified with B12, making it a popular supplement for plant-based diets.

description.en: Casein is the primary protein found in milk, making up about 80% of milk's protein content, and has been used for centuries in cheese-making across dairy-producing regions worldwide, since it's the protein that coagulates to form curds. It has a neutral, mildly milky flavor with no strong aroma, and forms a thick, slow-digesting texture when consumed—clumping into a gel in the stomach, unlike whey which stays liquid. Widely used in cheese production and as a slow-release protein supplement -particularly popular before bed among athletes-, casein is a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, along with calcium and phosphorus from its dairy origin.

description.en: Smoke is a collection of airborne solid and liquid particulates and gases emitted when a material undergoes combustion or pyrolysis, together with the quantity of air that is entrained or otherwise mixed into the mass. Smoke is sometimes used as a flavoring agent, and preservative for various foodstuffs. Smoking is the process of flavoring, browning, cooking, or preserving food by exposing it to smoke from burning or smoldering material, most often wood. Meat, fish, and lapsang souchong tea are often smoked.

Rice beans -Vigna umbellata- are a small, oval legume native to South and Southeast Asia, widely cultivated in northeast India, Nepal, Bhutan, southern China, Indonesia, and Thailand. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor and a texture similar to mung beans, cooking relatively quickly compared to other pulses. Across their growing regions, rice beans are used in soups, stews, curries, salads, and fermented dishes, and are sometimes sprouted or ground into flour. Nutritionally, they are valued as a good source of plant protein -notably rich in lysine, methionine, and tryptophan-, complex carbohydrates, dietary fiber, and minerals such as iron, zinc, and calcium.

description.en: Agave syrup -or agave nectar- is a liquid sweetener extracted from the core of the agave plant, particularly Agave tequilana, with production centered in Mexico where the plant has long been used to make traditional sweeteners and beverages like pulque. It has a mild, neutral sweetness—often noted as sweeter than honey—with subtle caramel notes in darker varieties, and a thin, smooth, honey-like texture that dissolves easily in cold liquids. Popular as a vegan honey substitute in beverages, baking, and dressings, agave syrup is very high in fructose -often 70-90%-, giving it a low glycemic index despite being calorie-dense, though its fructose concentration has raised similar metabolic concerns as high-fructose corn syrup.

description.en: Sourdough is a naturally leavened bread made using a fermented starter of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria rather than commercial yeast, a method dating back thousands of years to ancient Egypt and still central to regional baking traditions like San Francisco's tangy loaves. It has a distinctive tangy, slightly sour flavor with a chewy, dense crumb and crisp, often blistered crust, shaped by the specific microbial culture of its starter, which can vary by region and even household. Made simply from flour, water, salt, and the starter culture, sourdough's slow fermentation is thought to improve digestibility and lower the glycemic impact compared to conventionally leavened bread, while offering fiber, B vitamins, and modest protein from the flour base.

description.en: Raising agents are substances added to baked goods to produce carbon dioxide gas and create rise and lightness, with early forms like yeast used since ancient Egyptian times, while chemical versions such as baking soda and baking powder were developed in the 19th century as faster, more reliable alternatives. They are essentially flavorless or very mildly bitter/metallic on their own, though excess use can leave a soapy or tinny aftertaste, and they work by releasing gas bubbles that get trapped in dough or batter, creating a light, airy texture. Used across breads, cakes, and pastries—commonly as baking soda, baking powder, yeast, or ammonium bicarbonate—raising agents are used in such small quantities that they contribute negligible calories or nutrients, functioning purely as a leavening tool rather than a nutritional ingredient.

description.en: Brown Rajmah -brown kidney beans- traces its origins to the Andean highlands of the Americas, from where it spread globally and became widely cultivated across South Asia, especially in Kashmir and northern India. It has a light tan-brown skin with a mild, nutty, slightly earthy flavor and a firmer texture than red or black varieties. Commonly simmered in spiced curries, added to soups, stews, salads, and rice dishes, it's valued in cuisines worldwide for its versatility. Nutritionally, brown rajmah offers plant-based protein, dietary fiber, complex carbohydrates, iron, magnesium, and folate, making it a nourishing legume across diverse global food cultures.

Apricots are stone fruits believed to have originated in China or Central Asia thousands of years ago, later spreading along the Silk Road through Persia and into the Mediterranean, where regions like Turkey and California became major modern producers. They have a delicate, sweet-tart flavor with subtle floral and honeyed notes, and a soft, velvety-skinned flesh that's juicy when ripe and firms into a chewy, concentrated sweetness when dried. Eaten fresh, dried, or used in jams, baking, and savory glazes, apricots are a good source of vitamin A -from beta-carotene-, vitamin C, and fiber, with dried apricots also offering a notable concentration of iron and potassium.

Nutritionally, it provides vitamin C, potassium, and dietary fiber, along with natural sugars and antioxidant compounds, making it a commonly consumed seasonal stone fruit in temperate regions worldwide.

description.en: Protein is a macronutrient made of amino acid chains, sourced from a wide range of foods—animal sources like meat, fish, eggs, and dairy, and plant sources like legumes, grains, nuts, and soy—with humans relying on food-derived protein since prehistoric times as one of the three core macronutrients alongside fats and carbohydrates. Its flavor and texture vary enormously by source, from the rich, savory taste of meats to the neutral, often bland profile of isolated protein powders, which are typically processed from whey, soy, or pea into fine, mixable forms. Essential for building and repairing muscle, enzymes, and hormones, protein is measured by its amino acid completeness—animal proteins and a few plant sources like quinoa and soy are "complete," containing all nine essential amino acids, while most other plant proteins must be combined to achieve the same profile.

description.en: Moth beans -Vigna aconitifolia-, also called mat beans or matki, originated in the Indian subcontinent, where they've been cultivated for centuries as a hardy, drought-resistant crop suited to arid regions. Small, olive-brown, and oblong, they carry an earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a firm bite once cooked. Across South Asia, they're prepared whole or sprouted—simmered into curries, stewed with spices, or featured in dishes like Maharashtra's misal; sprouted moth beans also appear in salads and street snacks. Globally, they're valued as a protein- and fiber-rich pulse, contributing iron, folate, and other minerals typical of legumes within diverse traditional cuisines.

Carissa -commonly known as natal plum- is a small, glossy red fruit native to southern Africa, particularly South Africa, growing on a spiny shrub traditionally used both as a food source and an ornamental hedge in its native range. It has a tart, slightly sweet flavor often compared to a mix of cranberry and strawberry, with a soft, juicy flesh surrounding small seeds, though the unripe fruit and other plant parts contain a milky sap that's toxic if consumed. Eaten fresh, or used in jams, jellies, and sauces once ripe, carissa is a good source of vitamin C and antioxidants, though it remains a minor, largely regional fruit outside southern Africa.

description.en: Vital wheat gluten is a concentrated protein extracted from wheat flour by washing away the starch, a process refined industrially in the 20th century to create a versatile baking additive. On its own it's bland and neutral in flavor, though it develops a chewy, meaty texture when hydrated and cooked. It's used to boost elasticity and rise in bread dough, and is a key ingredient in seitan and other plant-based meat substitutes. It carries a robust, herbaceous flavor with piney, slightly peppery, and mildly bitter notes. Commonly used as a natural antioxidant and preservative in processed meats, oils, snacks, and sauces, it helps extend shelf life by slowing oxidation. Nutritionally, rosemary extract contains trace polyphenols and antioxidant compounds, though it's typically used in amounts too small to contribute meaningfully to daily nutrient intake.

description.en: Isomaltooligosaccharide -IMO- is a short-chain carbohydrate composed of glucose units linked in branched α-1‚6 bonds, found in trace amounts in fermented foods like miso, soy sauce, and sake, and produced commercially through enzymatic conversion of starch, a technology pioneered and widely commercialized in Japan since the 1980s. It has a mild sweetness, roughly 40-60% as sweet as sucrose, with a clean flavor and syrupy texture similar to corn syrup, making it a popular sugar substitute in protein bars, baked goods, and "low-sugar" products. Marketed as a prebiotic fiber that partially resists digestion and supports gut bacteria, IMO provides fewer calories than sucrose, though recent research has questioned how much of it is truly fermented in the colon versus digested as regular glucose, making its fiber and metabolic benefits somewhat contested.

description.en: Swordfish is a large, fast-swimming ocean fish -Xiphias gladius- known for the long, flat, sword-like bill it uses to slash at prey. As food, it's prized for a few distinct qualities: Texture and flavor: The flesh is firm, meaty, and dense — often compared to a good steak more than to flakier white fish. The flavor is mild but slightly rich, with a subtle sweetness; Cut and cooking: It's usually sold as thick steaks rather than fillets, since the loin is large. It grills, broils, or pan-sears very well, and holds up on skewers -it's a common choice for kebabs-; Fat content: It's a moderately fatty fish, which helps keep it moist during high-heat cooking like grilling — unlike very lean white fish that dry out easily.
